title: C482/167/2016 of Chetan Balutia Vs State Of Uttarakhand AND ANOTHER

paras.text:
Reserved Judgment
 REPORTABLE
IN THE HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Criminal Misc. Application No. 167 of 2016
Chetan Balutia ......Petitioner
Vs.
State of Uttarakhand and Another .... Respondents
Present:-Mr. Arvind Vashistha, Sr. Advocate, assisted by Mr. Hemant Singh Mehra, Advocate for the
petitioner.
 Mr. S.S. Adhikari, A.G.A for the State of Uttarakhand.
Mr. Harshit Sanwal, Advocate, holding brief of Mr. R.S. Sammal, Advocate for respondent
 No.2.
Hon'ble Ravindra Maithani, J.
The instant petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973 (for short 'the Code') has been filed to quash the order
dated 26.09.2015 passed in Criminal Revision No. 74 of 2013, Chetan
Balutia Vs. State and Others, by the court of Additional Sessions Judge - II,
Haldwani, District Nainital (for short 'the revision').
2. By the impugned order, while allowing an application under
Section 31-B filed by Ms. Margit Gunilla Balutia, she was permitted to
continue the criminal proceedings.
3. Facts necessary to decide the controversy, briefly stated, are as
hereunder:-
Respondent no.2 filed a complaint under Section 138 of the
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (for short 'the Act') and under Section
420 IPC against the petitioner, through power of attorney holder Pankaj
Kapri on the basis of which, proceedings of Criminal Case No. 1059 of

2
2013, Kailash Chandra Balutia Vs. Chetan Balutiya was instituted in the
court of learned Special Judicial Magistrate, Haldwani (for short 'the case').
After enquiry on 05.03.2013, petitioner was summoned under
Section 138 of the Act. It is this order summoning the petitioner, which was
challenged by him in the revision. During the pendency of the revision, an
application under Section 31-B was filed by Ms. Margit Gunilla Balutia for
substitution stating therein that her husband Kailash Chandra Balutiya died.
Petitioner filed objection to the application filed by Ms.
Margit Gunilla Balutia. According to the objections, Late Shri. Kailash
Chandra Balutiya, by executing a will dated 30.09.2013, had divested Ms.
Margit Gunilla Balutia from his property. Therefore Ms. Margit Gunilla
Balutia could not be permitted to continue with the prosecution. It was also
objected to that Late Shri. Kailash Chandra Balutiya was holder in due
course of the cheque but immediately after his death, the legal title vested in
him ceased and no right was assigned by him to his wife Ms. Margit Gunilla
Balutia in respect of cheque in question.
4. After hearing the parties, by the impugned order, the learned
court below allowed the application under section 31-B filed by Ms. Margit
Gunilla Balutia and permitted her to continue with the prosecution. This
order is impugned.
5. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the record.
6. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner raised the following
points in his arguments:-
(1) Ms. Margit Gunilla Balutia had already been divested of all movable and
immovable property by Late Shri. Kailash Chandra Balutia. The judgment
in the case of Ashwin Nanubhai Vyas Vs. The State of Maharashtra and
Another, AIR 1967 SC 983 is not applicable in the instant case because

3
instant is a summon case and the principles which were laid down in the
case of Ashwin (supra) related to warrant trial.
(2) Only a person who has right to continue the prosecution can seek
substitution. Reference has been made to the principles of law as laid down
in the case of Jimmy Jahangir Madan Vs. Bolly Cariyappa Hindley (Dead)
By LRS., (2004) 12 SCC 509.
(3) The offence under section 138 of the Act is essentially an offence against
movable property of the deceased and it is not an offence against the
person, therefore, it is argued that substitution application cannot be filed
by a person who has been divested of the property by the deceased.
Substitution application since not filed in the case, therefore, such
application cannot be entertained in the revision.
7. On behalf of respondent no.2, learned counsel would submit
that in the revision, the court may permit any person to address it. Moreover,
Ms. Margit Gunilla Balutia is wife of Late Shri. Kailash Chandra Balutia;
even in summon case, the court may permit a person to continue the
prosecution. If substitution is allowed and wife of deceased is permitted to
continue the prosecution, it does not prejudice anyone; Ms. Margit Gunilla
Balutia was not divested from the property by deceased Late Shri. Kailash
Chandra Balutia, instead, it is she who distanced herself from the property of
Late Shri. Kailash Chandra Balutia; the cheque in question was not covered
by the will issued by Late Shri. Kailash Chandra Balutia. Learned counsel
would argue that the impugned order is valid in the eyes of law and no
interference is warranted.
8. At the very outset, when the argument began, the Court wanted
to know from the learned counsel for the parties as to what was the need of
substitution in the revision. It is so because once admitted, the revision has to
be decided on merits and death of any of the parties makes no difference in

4
this regard, as held in the case of Pranab Kumar Mitra Vs. State of West
Bengal and Another, AIR 1959 SC 144.
Learned counsel for the respondent no.2 would submit to it that
even if substitution is made, it will also not make any difference.
9. In the case of Pranab Kumar (supra), Hon'ble Supreme Court,
inter alia, held that "whether it was an accused person or it was a
complainant who has moved the High Court in its revisional jurisdiction, if
the High Court has issued a Rule, that Rule has to be heard and determined in
accordance with law, whether or not the petitioner in the High Court is alive or
dead, or whether he is represented in court by a legal practitioner." (para 6)
10. In the instant case, even if the death of Late Shri. Kailash
Chandra Balutia would not have stopped continuance of the revision, but, at
the same time, if any person is allowed to continue, it also does not make any
difference. The question is whether the person, so allowed to continue with
the prosecution, has rightly been permitted to do so? To that extent, the
controversy will now be resolved. It is Section 302 of the Code which
permits continuance of prosecution by any person. It reads as hereunder:-
302. Permission to conduct prosecution. - (1) Any Magistrate inquiring into or
trying a case may permit the prosecution to be conducted by any person other than
a police officer below the rank of Inspector; but no person, other than the
Advocate General or Government Advocate or a Public Prosecutor or Assistant
Public Prosecutor, shall be entitled to do so without such permission:
Provided that no police officer shall be permitted to conduct the
prosecution if he has taken part in the investigation into the offence with respect to
which the accused is being prosecuted.

5
(2) Any person conducting the prosecution may do so personally or by a
pleader.
11. The instant case arises from proceedings under section 138 of
the Act. It is a summon case. Undoubtedly under section 256 of the Code, in
the non-appearance of the complainant, the accused may be acquitted unless
for some reason, the Magistrate thinks it proper to adjourn hearing to some
other day. The proviso to Section 256 of the Code makes it more elaborate
that even in the absence of complainant, how the case may be heard? The
proviso to Section 256 of the Code is as hereunder:-
"256. Non- appearance or death of complainant. -
(1) .........................................
Provided that where the complainant is represented by a pleader or by the
officer conducting the prosecution or where the Magistrate is of opinion that the
personal attendance of the complainant is not necessary, the Magistrate may
dispense with his attendance and proceed with the case.
(2) The provisions of sub- section (1) shall, so far as may be, apply also to
cases where the non- appearance of the complainant is due to his death."
12. An argument has been advanced that in the case of Ashwin
(supra), principles have been laid down in the warrant trial, therefore, they
would not be attracted in the instant case, because it is a summon case and
death of the complainant will result in the acquittal of the petitioner.
13. This argument has no substance for the simple reason that
Section 302 of the Code does not distinguish between summon case and
warrant case. Moreover, under Section 256 of the Code, even on the death of
the complainant, it is not necessary that the accused may be acquitted. The
Court will still continue with the prosecution notwithstanding the death of

6
the complainant. Similar arguments were advanced in the case of Balasaheb
K. Thackeray and Another Vs. Venkat @ Bablu and Another, (2006) 5 SCC
530 (paragraph 3 of the judgment). But this argument was not accepted.
What the Court held in the case of Balasaheb K. Thackeray (supra) was that
"to bring an application of Section 302 of the Code, permission to conduct
the prosecution has to be obtained from the Magistrate inquiring into or
trying case." (Paragraph 6).
14. It has also been argued on behalf of the petitioner that the
prosecution may be continued only by the person who has "right to
continue" and reference has been made to the judgment in the case of Jimmy
Jahangir (supra). Paragraph 9 of it is as hereunder:-
"9. The language of Sections 205 and 302 of the Code is similar. Under Section
302 of the Code, a party can make an application himself to continue the
prosecution or the same can be made by a pleader. As provided under Section
2(q) of the Code, the prayer to continue the prosecution can be made either by a
legally qualified person, who is authorised to practise in the court under
the Advocates Act; or by any other person which would obviously include a
power of attorney holder in which eventuality such permission can be granted by
the court where the prosecution is pending only if it is sought by the person who is
entitled to continue the prosecution and not by the power of attorney holder.
Under Section 205 of the Code, an accused is required to appear in person but his
personal appearance can be dispensed with and he can be allowed to be
represented by a pleader. Likewise, under Section 302 of the Code, a person, who
is entitled to continue the prosecution, is required to make an application himself
but under both the provisions aforesaid, instead of taking steps personally, a party
can be represented through a pleader. Power of attorney holder can represent the
concerned party under both the provisions of the Code, in case permission for
such representation is sought from the court by the concerned person and granted
by it. But where no such permission is sought by the concerned person, meaning

7
thereby, in the case of Section 205 of the Code an accused and in the case
of Section 302 of the Code a party who has right to continue the prosecution,
power of attorney holder cannot be allowed to represent the concerned person in
the proceeding."
(Emphasis supplied)
15. In the case of Ashwin (supra), an argument was raised that if
the Court provides that cognizance may be taken on the complaint of a
specified person, the continuance of the proceedings may also be done by the
same person. It was argued that "if cognizance could not be taken unless a
complaint was made in the manner provided in the section, the Court cannot
proceed with the inquiry unless the same condition continues to exist. This
argument was not accepted. Hon'ble Court held that "the section creates a
bar which has to be removed before cognizance is taken. Once the bar is
removed, because the proper person has filed a complaint, the section works
itself out. If any other restriction was also there, the Code would have said
so. Not having said so, one must treat the section as fulfilled and work out."
(Paragraph 7)
16. It is true that in the case of Jimmy Jahangir (supra), Hon'ble
Court held that under Section 302 of the Code, a party who has right to
continue the prosecution may seek permission to continue prosecution and
not the Power of Attorney holder. The question in the case of Jimmy
Jahangir (supra) was whether Power of Attorney holder can be treated to be
a pleader of heirs of the complainant? (Paragraph 5 last lines) and in that
context, the observations have been made as quoted in paragraph 9
hereinabove.

8
17. Section 302 of the Code does not lay down that only legal
representatives or heirs of the deceased may continue with the prosecution.
According to Section 302 of the Code, any person may be permitted by the
Code to conduct the prosecution subject to the limitation as given in the
Section itself. The words "any person" is significant. It is true that offence
under Section 138 of the Act is person specific and it relates to property but
does it mean that a person who has no right in the property cannot be
permitted prosecution under Section 138 of the Act. It is also true that
cognizance under Section 138 of the Act may be taken, only upon a
complaint in writing made by a payee, or as the case may be, the holder in
due course of the cheque provided under Section 142 of the Act, but, if
Section 142 of the Act is read along with Section 256 and Section 302 of the
Code, it is not mandatory that after the death of the complainant, the
prosecution must be continued by a person who has interest in the property
of the deceased or who is legal heir of the deceased.
18. It is argued that the deceased Kailash Chandra Balutiya had
divested Ms. Margit Gunilla Balutia from his property. A Will has been
referred to in this regard. It is true that, according to the copy of the Will,
Ms. Margit Gunilla Balutia has not been given any share in any movable or
immovable property in India because according to the Will itself, Ms. Margit
Gunilla Balutia, who is Swedish National, was not interested in such
property. Moreover, the cheque in question is not part of the Will. Therefore,
at the strength of the Will of the deceased Kailash Chandra Balutiya also, it
cannot be said that Ms. Margit Gunilla Balutia, cannot conduct the
prosecution.

9
19. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner would also submit
that since substitution has not been made in the case, substitution cannot be
allowed in revision. This argument has no force. Revision was proceeding at
the relevant time and substitution made. As and when the case proceeds, the
continuance of the case may be considered then.
20. Therefore, this Court is of the view that the Court may under
Section 302 of the Code permit any person to continue the prosecution under
Section 138 of the Act, subject to the limitations given under Section 302 of
the Code itself. In the instant case, Ms. Margit Gunilla Balutia is wife of
deceased Kailash Chandra Balutiya. She has every right to continue with the
prosecution and this Court is of the view that learned court below did not
commit any error in allowing application 31(B) of Ms. Margit Gunilla
Balutia to continue the prosecution. There is no substance in the petition.
21. The petition is dismissed.
 (Ravindra Maithani, J.)
 05.06.2020
Ujjwal
